notes.meaning: After Joshua died, the people of Israel had no single human leader to guide them. They did what was right by asking the Lord who should lead the fight against the remaining Canaanites. They likely sought God's guidance through the high priest. When big changes happen in life, turning first to God brings true direction.

The Lord chose the tribe of Judah to go first and promised to give them victory. Judah was the largest and strongest tribe, and Jacob had long ago foretold that Judah would lead his brothers. God matches the work He assigns to the strength He provides.

Judah asked their neighboring brother tribe, Simeon, to join them in the fight, promising to help them in return. Simeon's land sat inside Judah's borders, making them natural partners. Even the strongest believers benefit from joining hands with others to serve God.

Judah and Simeon marched out, and the Lord gave them a great victory over ten thousand enemy fighters at Bezek. Their success came from God fulfilling His promise, not merely from their own weapons. When God's people move forward in obedience, He works on their behalf.

During the campaign, the Israelites clashed with Adoni-bezek, the ruler of that city. His title means 'lord of Bezek.' He led the Canaanite and Perizzite armies against Israel but was soundly defeated.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest Adoni-bezek may be another name or spelling for Adoni-zedek, the king of Jerusalem mentioned in Joshua 10.

notes.meaning: When Adoni-bezek tried to run away, the Israelites caught him and cut off his thumbs and big toes. This was done to disable him so he could never hold a weapon or run in battle again. It also stripped him of his power as a warrior king.

Adoni-bezek admitted that he had done this exact cruelty to seventy other kings and made them beg for crumbs under his table. He recognized that God was giving him the exact punishment he deserved. The men of Judah brought him to Jerusalem, where he eventually died.

differ.view: Letting Adoni-bezek live and bringing him to Jerusalem was a failure to obey God's clear command to put Canaanite leaders entirely to death.

notes.meaning: The men of Judah attacked Jerusalem, captured it, struck down its defenders, and set the city on fire. While they burned the city, the Jebusites still held on to their strong fortress on the hill. Complete control of Jerusalem would not come until the time of King David.

Next, the army of Judah moved out to clear the Canaanites from other regions of their allotted land. They fought across the mountains, the dry southern desert called the Negev, and the western foothills. They were taking active steps to claim what God had assigned to them.

Judah marched against the ancient city of Hebron, once called Kiriath-arba, and defeated three giant leaders living there. These descendants of Anak had terrified Israel's spies a generation earlier. Faith in God overcame the giants that once caused Israel to tremble in fear.

From Hebron, the forces of Judah pressed on to fight the people of Debir, which used to be called Kiriath-sepher. This city was another fortified stronghold in the hill country. Taking it was vital to securing the southern region.

Caleb offered his daughter Acsah in marriage to whoever showed the courage to attack and take the city of Kiriath-sepher. His nephew Othniel took up the challenge, captured the city, and won Acsah as his wife. Caleb sought to pass on bold faith to the next generation, and Othniel later served as Israel's first judge.

Acsah urged her new husband to ask her father for a field, and then she boldly approached Caleb herself. She explained that since her land in the dry south needed water, she also needed springs to make it fertile. Caleb gladly answered her request by giving her both upper and lower springs, showing how a loving father delights to give good gifts.

The relatives of Moses' father-in-law, known as the Kenites, moved with the people of Judah from Jericho into the southern desert near Arad. They chose to live peacefully alongside Judah in tents. God kept His old promise to welcome and care for those who joined His people.

Judah kept their promise to Simeon by going with them to destroy the Canaanite city of Zephath. They completely devoted the city to destruction as had been vowed years earlier, naming it Hormah. Keeping promises to our brothers brings shared victory.

Judah also pushed west toward the coast and captured three major Philistine cities: Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, along with their surrounding land. Even though they took these cities, they did not wipe out the inhabitants completely. Because of this, the Philistines soon took these cities back and remained a thorn in Israel's side.

The Lord helped Judah take the hill country, but they failed to drive out the people living in the plains because those enemies had iron chariots. The problem was not that the chariots were stronger than God, but that Judah's fear overcame their faith. When believers look at the size of their obstacles instead of God's power, they lose ground.

As Moses had promised long before, the city of Hebron was given to Caleb as his personal inheritance. Caleb drove out the three giant sons of Anak who lived there. Caleb's lifelong trust in God proved that God's promises never fail.

The tribe of Benjamin failed to drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem, so the Jebusites continued living right beside them. Jerusalem sat on the border between Judah and Benjamin, and neither tribe finished the job of clearing the city. Compromising with spiritual enemies allows danger to remain close at hand.

The tribes of Joseph—Ephraim and western Manasseh—went up to attack the city of Bethel, and the Lord was with them. Before attacking, they sent scouts to spy out the city, which was originally called Luz. God's presence gave them confidence, but they still planned their actions with practical care.

The scouts spotted a man leaving Bethel and promised to spare his life and family if he showed them an entrance into the city. He revealed a weak or hidden entrance, and the Israelites captured Bethel and struck it down, keeping their word to protect the man's family. While Israel honored their pledge of mercy, the man chose survival over true devotion to Israel's God.

After being released, the man traveled to the land of the Hittites and built a new city, naming it Luz after his old home. Unlike Rahab, who chose to become part of God's covenant people, this man simply went back to his old pagan way of life. Sparing external enemies often led to pagan culture reviving elsewhere.

The tribe of Manasseh failed to clear out Beth-shean, Megiddo, and several other towns, along with their surrounding villages. The Canaanites were determined to hold on to these strategic trade towns in the valley. Manasseh backed down instead of trusting God for complete victory.

When the Israelites grew stronger, they forced the Canaanites into hard labor instead of driving them out as God had commanded. They chose the financial and practical benefits of forced workers over wholehearted obedience to God's law. Choosing personal profit over God's commands always leads to spiritual trouble.

Ephraim also failed to drive out the Canaanites who lived in the city of Gezer. Instead of finishing the fight, they let the Canaanites live right among them as neighbors. Incomplete obedience allowed pagan practices to take root in their own backyard.

The tribe of Zebulun failed to expel the inhabitants of Kitron and Nahalol. They settled for putting the Canaanites to forced labor and letting them stay in the land. Like their brother tribes, they chose economic convenience over full obedience.

Asher failed to drive out the people of important coastal cities like Acco and Sidon. The Canaanites were so strong that the Asherites ended up living among them as a minority rather than ruling the area. When believers give up the fight against sin, the world soon takes control.

Naphtali also failed to drive out the people of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath, two fortified cities. The people of Naphtali lived among the Canaanites, though they were eventually able to force them into labor. They settled for living with idolatry rather than removing it.

The Amorites pushed the tribe of Dan back into the hills and refused to let them settle the fertile valleys. Dan was unable to conquer their own inheritance, but the stronger tribes of Joseph later stepped in and forced these Amorites to pay tribute. Weakness and lack of faith cost Dan much of their God-given territory.

The territory of the Amorites stretched from the Scorpion Pass all the way past Sela and upward into the southern mountains. This note explains why the Amorites were so powerful and hard for Dan to defeat. Unchecked enemies established deep footholds that would trouble Israel for generations to come.
